# Perceptions of the role of dentists in HPV and COVID-19 vaccinations: Results of a cross-sectional validated survey of adults

**Authors:** Katherine France; Morgan Faist; Dana Kost; Yueping Luo; Jinbo Niu; Lake Seymour; Tamara Cadet

**Affiliations:** 1Assistant Professor of Oral Medicine, University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA | 2Student, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA | 3Dental Student, University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA | 4Business Intelligence Analyst, Strategic Research Insights, Inc, West Windsor Township, NJ, USA | 5Research Assistant, University of Pennsylvania School of Social Policy and Practice, Philadelphia, PA, USA | 6Orthodontic Resident, Harvard University School of Dental Medicine, Boston, MA, USA | 7Associate Professor, University of Pennsylvania School of Social Policy and Practice, Philadelphia, PA, USA, University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA

## Abstract

Human papillomavirus (HPV) and COVID-19 are contagious diseases for which effective vaccines exist. Dental involvement in vaccination campaigns for these conditions have been proposed but there is a lack of understanding of dentists’ roles in vaccination, specifically assessing attitudes around dentists as vaccinators for HPV and COVID-19.

Using a cross-sectional design and convenience sampling, a 12-item validated survey was distributed to community members to determine perceptions about dentist roles in vaccination for HPV and COVID-19. Demographics, vaccination status, knowledge of the diseases, vaccination intentions, and willingness to receive education, recommendation, and administration of vaccine from a dental provider were assessed. Responses were analyzed using bivariate and multivariate analysis.

Of 618 participants, most were previously vaccinated against HPV and COVID-19 (n=462, 75.6% and n=371, 61.0% respectively). Participants responded more favorably to dentist involvement in educating, discussing, and administering COVID-19 vaccines than HPV vaccines (p<0.05). Participant knowledge of HPV was found to be low compared to COVID-19. There were significant differences across demographic groups, with race most frequently associated with differences in response across COVID-19 and HPV-related questions.

This study provides formative data to develop interventions to support dentists’ participation in vaccination campaigns. Participant acceptance of COVID-19 vaccination over HPV vaccination may reflect the public awareness of COVID-19 versus HPV due to daily relevance of this disease, or the lack of knowledge about HPV, particularly its oropharyngeal impacts.

These results provide evidence to support dentist involvement in vaccine education and distribution, expanding previous literature into evaluation of a new disease context (COVID-19). Lack of knowledge of HPV may impact willingness to receive HPV vaccination efforts, presenting an opportunity for education.

## Introduction

The Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection (STI) in the United States (US).1,2 Spread through direct skin-to-skin contact during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, HPV can cause genital warts and certain types of cancers including cervical, vaginal, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers.1,3 Estimates indicate that 70% or more of oropharyngeal cancers are caused by HPV, more than any other body site.4,5 Gardasil 9 is a nonavalent vaccine against the most common strains of HPV and the only HPV vaccine distributed in the US. Recommendations suggest that two doses be administered at ages 9–12 with evidence suggesting higher completion rates for those that begin the series earlier.6,7 Teens and young adults through 26 years who have not been fully vaccinated are recommended to receive catch-up doses to prevent cancers caused by HPV. Catch-up vaccination is also recommended in adults 27–45 years old with a low chance of previous exposure to HPV.8 Limited data indicate that vaccines against HPV decrease rates of HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers, as is the case for cancers in other body sites.9,10,11

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a respiratory illness caused by SARS-CoV-2. It is spread by small droplets released from the mouth or nose of an infected individual when sneezing or coughing.12 There are currently three approved or authorized COVID-19 vaccines in the US, produced by Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, and Novavax. Immunization doses, timing, and booster doses vary depending on vaccine, age, and length of time since last dose.13 The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in necessary national restrictions intended to limit disease spread. These restrictions also impacted vaccine uptake and resulting rates of complete vaccination.14,15

Dental training and knowledge prepare dentists and dental students to be safe and effective providers of various health interventions who therefore can be included in the public health workforce.16,17 Dentists play primary roles as comprehensive healthcare providers in both disease prevention and health promotion.18 During the COVID-19 pandemic, to increase access to newly available COVID-19 vaccines, state regulations, supported by the federal government, allowed for dentists to administer vaccines.19,20 Although including dentists in COVID-19 efforts allowed rapid mobilization of a highly trained workforce, allowance for dentists to provide vaccines for other diseases, such as influenza has historically been limited.21 Only the state of Oregon had licensed dentists to provide all vaccines prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, while states such as Illinois and Minnesota had previously supported permanent expansion of dental services to include influenza vaccinations.22,23,24

Findings from previous studies examining individual and family perceptions of dentists provision of the HPV vaccine indicate that a majority of parents are open to discussion and receipt of immunizations by dental teams,25,26 although some existing evidence does identify variations in willingness.27,28 Additional studies have evaluated dentists’ perception of participating in vaccination campaigns, including administering HPV vaccines, showing comfort discussing and in some cases administering vaccines.29,30 However, more evidence is required to fully understand public perception of the roles dentists may play in diverse vaccination campaigns, and any variation in those responses. The comparison of HPV and COVID-19 vaccines in particular is appropriate as these diseases have made a profound impact on public health and therefore are relevant and salient contexts in which to consider expanding disease prevention. Given the sexual context and age limitations of HPV vaccines as well as the political context and varying dosing guidelines of COVID-19 vaccines, vaccination attitudes surrounding these diseases in the dental settings may be divergent, allowing for a more detailed and accurate understanding of patient perspectives around dentist roles in vaccination.

This study builds upon a previous pilot study that was the first to assess patient acceptance of dentist involvement in a vaccination campaign outside of HPV.31 Findings from Steinbaum et al. identified that a majority of patients would accept recommendation for COVID-19 and HPV vaccine, with responses differing according to race.31 This study aims to expand this evidence to determine the attitudes of community members around dentists as vaccinators using a validated survey instrument. The primary aim of this study is to identify differences between acceptance of vaccines for HPV and COVID-19. The secondary aim is to identify any difference in participant responses according to demographic factors.

## Methods

Using a cross-sectional design, this study aimed to determine the attitudes of community members around the role of dentists in COVID-19 and HPV vaccinations. Participants were included if they were between the ages of 18 and 45, spoke and read English, were able to provide their own verbal consent, and were willing to complete the survey. No other limitations, such as medical history, recent dental or medical treatment, or experience with vaccines were applied and none of this information was gathered. Our age range was defined according to the ages approved to receive catch-up HPV vaccinations to ensure relevance of all survey questions to the included participants. If subjects were willing to participate, the risks and benefits of completing the survey were reviewed, and verbal consent was obtained. Participants were informed that the survey was estimated to take less than 10 minutes and were provided unlimited time to take the survey. Contact information for the survey team, introductory information on the survey, and background about the two diseases covered was provided before starting the survey questions (Supplement 1). The surveys were completed on iPads maintained by our institution using the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) management system.32 After completing the survey, all participants received a $20 gift card to thank them for their time and a handout with information about HPV and COVID-19 to add to the educational value of this survey.

A convenience sample of survey responses was collected by a team of four trained research assistants in Philadelphia over the month of July 2022. The survey collection took place in public locations including coffee shops, parks, and health centers to maximize the variation in respondent demographics and attitudes. All research assistants were trained in appropriate conduct of research, study design, and participant eligibility, and utilized scripts in approaching subjects for participation. Flyers describing the survey were posted around Philadelphia and on institutional social media to recruit participants and provided to participants to distribute within their networks. Based on existing data on acceptance,23 a sample size of 600 was planned to elucidate a 10% difference in acceptance between vaccines (n=582, 80% power, alpha=0.05, beta=0.10). This utilized both pilot data and data from alternate settings which estimated approximately 80% acceptance for dentists as providers of HPV vaccines. The power calculation was a conservative estimate as it assumed participants may complete only questions about one of the vaccines (COVID-19 or HPV), leaving half of the survey blank. The survey instrument was developed through content and psychometric validation of a previously distributed survey (further data on validation available on request).31 The results reported here are from the final survey, which included demographics (gender and gender identity, age, race, education level, and household income); five questions per disease (HPV and COVID-19) assessing vaccination status and future intention, understanding of the impacts of the disease, and willingness to receive education, recommendation, and administration of a vaccine from a dental provider. The final survey instrument is available as Supplement 2. No personally identifying information was collected during or after the survey and no follow-up with the patients was completed.

All survey data was analyzed using Python (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA), R software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), and Microsoft Excel (Redmond, WA, USA). We conducted descriptive analyses for the demographic factors. An initial exploratory analysis confirmed that the collected data violated the assumption of normality. To evaluate our primary aim of determining if there was any difference in attitudes between the two diseases, differences between answers relating to the COVID-19 and HPV vaccines were compared for each question using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. For the questions about whether a dentist could educate, discuss, and administer vaccines for each disease, we coded 1 as ‘yes,’ 0 as ‘unsure,’ and −1 as ‘no’ to confirm that the averages were not skewed by ‘unsure’. To evaluate the impact of demographic variables on responses, a series of chi-squared tests were conducted for categorical variables to assess how perceptions varied across groups. Given the small number of participants whose gender identities diverged from their sex identified at birth, only sex assigned at birth was used for analysis. Spearman correlation was employed to determine the relationship between continuous variables (age) and question responses. A multivariate logistic regression was completed across all demographic features. This allowed us to address our secondary aim of determining how perceptions varied according to demographic factors. Significance was set at p<0.05. After removing entries that were blank or only included demographic data, we analyzed 618 survey responses that contained answers to at least one set of disease-specific questions.

This project received Institutional Review Board approval under expedited review (protocol #850769).

## Results

### Descriptive Analysis

The mean age of participants was 28.09 with a range between 18–45 years. The majority of participants were female (n=397, 64.2%). Participants identified with all racial categories, with the largest percentages selecting White (n=267, 43.3%) and African American/Black (n=179, 29.1%). The largest percentage of participants had bachelor’s degrees (n=219, 35.6%) with 24.6% (n=151) having incomes over $100,000 (See Table 1).

Most participants had received all recommended COVID-19 and HPV vaccination doses (n=462, 75.6% and n=371, 61.0% respectively). A large majority of subjects (n=559, 91.6%) had been informed that the COVID-19 vaccine could prevent severe illness caused by COVID-19. A much smaller majority of subjects had been informed that the HPV vaccine could prevent some types of head and neck cancer (n=328, 53.9%). Responses to each of the survey questions are shown in Figure 1 and Table 2, which illustrates numerical differences in response to each question when asked in relation to COVID-19 and to HPV.

### Bivariate Analysis

Table 3 presents the comparison of differences in responses between questions about COVID-19 and HPV. The results of Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that there were significant differences between people’s perception towards COVID-19 and HPV across each metric asked. Questions about whether respondents saw dentists as able to educate, discuss, and administer vaccines yielded significantly higher positive answers about COVID-19 than about HPV (p<0.05). Participants’ knowledge, evaluated according to whether participants had been informed about the impact of the diseases and vaccines, showed the biggest difference among the questions. Participants’ knowledge of COVID-19 vaccines in preventing severe disease was higher than that of HPV vaccines (p<0.05). Participants also demonstrated significantly higher vaccination rates and future plans associated with COVID-19 than they did for HPV (p<0.05).

Table 4 presents how the participants’ perceptions towards the two vaccines varied across different demographic groups using chi-squared tests. These results identified race as the most statistically significant factor in differentiating perceptions. There were statistically significant differences between racial groups across all questions except willingness to discuss COVID-19 vaccines with dentists (p=0.077). Income was found to be associated with different levels of previous vaccination, willingness to discuss HPV vaccination, and openness to receiving COVID-19 vaccination from dentists (p<0.05 for listed attributes). Education level was associated with COVID-19 vaccination status, HPV knowledge, and willingness to accept COVID-19 vaccination by a dentist (p=0.01, p=0.01, p=0.049, respectively). Sex assigned at birth was associated only with COVID-19 and HPV vaccination status (p=0.006 and p=0.001, respectively).

### Multivariate Logistic Regression

Demographic factors were analyzed using multivariate logistic regression to identify predictors of response to each question. Increasing age was associated with lower vaccination status for HPV (Table 5). Income was not a significant predictor of any responses. Increasing levels of education increased the likelihood of participants reporting higher COVID-19 vaccination status and previous knowledge about HPV. Female respondents reported higher COVID-19 and HPV vaccination statuses, but lower willingness to allow a dentist to administer an HPV vaccine. African American participants reported lower levels of vaccination status than White participants for both COVID-19 and HPV (OR [CI] (p) for African American participants compared to White participants=0.33 [0.20, 0.54] (p<0.001) for COVID-19, 0.59 [0.38, 0.92] (p=0.02)), were less likely to report COVID-19 knowledge (0.18 [0.07, 0.56] (p<0.001)), were less likely to report openness to HPV education (0.55 [0.36, 0.83] (p=0.01)), discussion (0.60 [0.39, 0.93] (p=0.02)), and vaccination by dentists (0.41 [0.27, 0.63] (p<0.001)), and were less likely to be open to COVID-19 vaccination by dentists (0.36 [0.23, 0.59] (p<0.001)). Asian participants were more likely than Whites to report previous knowledge of HPV (OR [CI] (p) for Asian participants compared to White participants=1.74 [1.07, 2.82] (p=0.03)) and to be comfortable discussing COVID-19 vaccines with dentists (1.92 [1.02, 3.60] (p=0.04)). Other races were less likely than Whites to report full COVID-19 and HPV vaccination (OR [CI] (p) for participants of other races compared to White participants=0.46 [0.23, 0.91] (p=0.03) for COVID-19 and 0.49 [0.28, 0.87] (p=0.02) for HPV), previous COVID-19 knowledge (0.21 [0.07, 0.63] (p=0.01)), and accept either COVID-19 or HPV vaccination from dentists (0.52 [0.28, 0.98] (p=0.04) for COVID-19 and 0.55 [0.32, 0.95] (p=0.03) for HPV).

## Discussion

This study aimed to determine community perceptions around dentist involvement in vaccination efforts via convenience sampling in a large metropolitan area. This study is distinct from other similar investigations in comparing responses across two different vaccine-preventable diseases, which novelly allows for distinction in how respondents may view dental involvement in vaccination efforts generally as compared to disease-specific responses.25,26 In this way, these data expand previously available information, adding evidence to the American Dental Association resolution suggesting that dentists administer vaccines in order to advance public health.33

Overall, survey participants were vaccinated against COVID-19 and HPV at high rates with those not previously vaccinated divided in their future vaccine intention and willingness. Participants were also found to be overall aware of the impact of both COVID-19 and HPV; the majority of participants were aware of the impact of COVID-19 while a little more than half were aware of the connection between HPV and oropharyngeal cancer. This reflects variability in responses generally and specifically when comparing responses about COVID-19 and HPV, with participants significantly more likely to understand the impact of COVID-19. This difference between COVID-19 and HPV is maintained throughout our data, with adults in our sample not only more aware of the impact of COVID-19, but also more likely to agree that dentists may have a role in educating, discussing, and administering COVID-19 vaccines. Higher acceptance of dentists’ roles in COVID-19 vaccination may then be related to higher awareness and knowledge of this disease given the worldwide societal impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. Hesitancy around HPV compared to around COVID-19 could also be due to concerns about sexual health privacy and stigma, particularly for those who do not understand the connection between HPV and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.34

Previous studies have connected a lack of accurate and complete information and spread of misinformation to vaccine hesitancy.35 While vaccine hesitancy has been explored in previous papers and has been recognized as a growing threat to disease prevention, our study population overall was widely accepting of the dentist’s role in vaccination efforts.36,37,38 This overall support existed despite the lack of Pennsylvania policy allowing dentists to administer vaccinations. Findings from our study reinforce those from our previous pilot study, which suggested overall willingness to accept vaccinations from dental providers in a similar population.31 Incorporation of dentists in vaccination efforts could expand access to vaccines and increase preventative care efforts for both HPV and COVID-19. This expansion of the workforce is critical since increasing accessibility of vaccination is a known approach to raising vaccination rates.39 Findings from previous studies have further identified that dentists can reach a younger population, including adolescents, who typically make limited visits to their physicians. Expanded roles for dentists in vaccine administration may then be able to work across the three tiers of change: education, dentist participation, and institutional preparedness.18

Answers to our survey questions varied according to demographic factors, with the most differences seen in comparison of different racial groups. Asian participants showed increased willingness over Whites to discuss COVID-19 vaccines with dentists and increased previous knowledge of HPV, with a trend toward increased agreement across questions about HPV vaccines. Some previous research among the Asian-American population has shown a similar positive attitude toward HPV vaccination, while also identifying understanding and access as factors that could limit uptake, with variability by subgroup.40,41 Responses by African American or Black adults, however, demonstrated the opposite trend, toward negative or unsure responses across questions about both COVID-19 and HPV vaccines, with the willingness to be educated about, discuss, or receive an HPV vaccine and receive a COVID-19 vaccine from a dentist significantly below responses of White participants. This may relate to long standing racial disparities in healthcare increasingly recognized in light of the COVID-19 pandemic.42 While these disparities and the resultant lack of trust have been repeatedly found to apply to both Black and Asian patients, historical treatment of Black Americans’ health and the resulting lack of trust may explain the differences in attitudes in our study.43 Given the long-term psychological impact of studies such as the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, Black and African American community trust of new initiatives that may be perceived as experimental is often particularly low.44,45 These disparities are found to apply to HPV vaccine uptake generally, with low levels of trust in providers, government agencies, and pharmaceutical companies resulting in low HPV vaccination rates in one review.46 Given these historical factors, however, efforts to increase vaccination awareness and provision remain essential and may allow for dentists to build knowledge and consideration of vaccines.

This study does have limitations, including a using population from a single large urban area with a cross-sectional design. This could lead to selection bias and the inability to account for changing attitudes over time. Generalizing the data from this specific population also may not encompass the differences in attitude seen from other regions within the state and country.

## Conclusion

Despite the limitations, our study results suggest overall willingness to include dentists in vaccination efforts, including through education, discussion, and administration of vaccines. This study adds to the growing evidence on acceptance of dentist involvement in vaccine efforts by utilizing both COVID-19 and HPV as example vaccinations, allowing for a unique comparison of responses between these two contexts. In order to inform further efforts to expand these important preventive services, we also examined the role of demographic factors such as race, education, and income in influencing responses to dentists’ involvement in vaccine distribution. The knowledge gap observed between COVID-19 and HPV may provide an opportunity for dentists to provide education on HPV, its vaccine, and its importance, such as through targeted campaigns focused on increasing public awareness of the connection between HPV and oropharyngeal cancer. Variability in responses across demographic groups also identifies possible roles for dentists to educate on a micro level with patients and on a macro level advocating for policy. Future research should explore these variations and continue to identify barriers dentists face in providing vaccination efforts. These efforts will lead to evidence-based interventions that can seek to build trust across populations, educate patients, and ultimately ensure that communities are healthier thanks to the efforts of dentists in expanded roles.
